title: lock and Monitor
description: Use the lock statement and Monitor class to protect shared state from concurrent access.

data.text: The `lock` keyword is the simplest way to prevent two threads from executing the same block of code at the same time. Under the hood, it uses the `Monitor` class to acquire an exclusive lock on an object.

When a thread enters a `lock` block, it calls `Monitor.Enter` on the lock object. If another thread already holds that lock, the requesting thread blocks until the lock is released. When execution leaves the `lock` block (normally or via exception), `Monitor.Exit` is called automatically.

data.title: Basic lock usage

items: **Lock on public objects** — If external code can access your lock object, it can cause deadlocks or denial of service.
**Reentrancy** — The same thread can re-enter a `lock` it already holds. This is safe in single-threaded contexts but can mask design problems.
**Lock ordering** — Acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order across threads is a recipe for deadlock.

data.title: Deadlock caused by inconsistent lock ordering
Keep lock objects private
data.text: Always use a dedicated, private object for locking. Locking on `this`, `typeof(MyClass)`, or string literals exposes the lock to external code.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Lock objects should be private and dedicated.
Prefer fine-grained locks to reduce contention.
